extracted.intended_audience: short-story writers, creative-writing students, and literary readers interested in craft
extracted.subtask_description: Advice and standards for writing short stories and assembling short-story collections, drawn from an author interview about choices in voice, setting, sequencing, and use of personal material. Focuses on craft decisions for individual stories and for collections/novel-in-stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve each story's integrity over forcing collection fit
rubrics_metrics.description: “I am only interested in each story itself, and I worry about any compromise to a story’s integrity that’s performed to make it ‘fit’ into a collection.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alter or weaken a story in order to create artificial cohesion for a collection. Prioritize what each piece needs on its own rather than making editorial compromises to produce a thematic or structural fit across the book.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alphabetizing as a sequencing strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore: she loves alphabetizing and chose A–Z so 'stories [would] be next to one another that had never been adjacent... Perhaps new sparky conversations would occur.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sequencing choices affect reader experience; alphabetical order can create unexpected juxtapositions and makes stories easy to find by title. It is a valid alternative to chronological or collection-based organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat short stories as discrete units
rubrics_metrics.description: Short stories are often treated as discrete units; Moore focuses on each story itself rather than the collection-form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing and editing, ensure each story can stand alone—with its own arc, integrity, and completeness—unless the project is explicitly a connected sequence or novel-in-stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: If doing a novel-in-stories, think of stories as chapters
rubrics_metrics.description: “Now a novel-in-stories is a different matter, and one must then concern oneself with stories as chapters.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the project is a novel-in-stories, plan for inter-story cohesion, recurring arcs, and the kind of chapter-like functions stories must perform to build a larger narrative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the second-person can create streamlined, subjectless sentences
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore on second-person: she liked 'the subjectless syntax of the imperative: it’s a very streamlined sentence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Second-person (especially imperative) is a deliberate stylistic choice that can produce a concise, direct sentence rhythm. Be aware of its tone and historical associations (poems, letters, diaries) and use it intentionally rather than as a gimmick.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious about adopting web/social-media speech tics without authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: On web influence: Moore doesn't do social media and suggests social media is a 'terrible time-suck'; she reports hearing internet acronyms used by older people but does not treat social-media speech as an influence on her characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid gratuitous insertion of social-media idioms or speech tics unless they serve character and context. Authenticity matters more than trend-following.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make setting integral—use landscape, weather, and regional features
rubrics_metrics.description: Regarding place: Moore wanted 'landscape and weather and regional thisses and thats' to be part of her last two novels; place can function almost like a character.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete regional details and environmental features to shape tone, theme, and character. Setting can influence plot and psychological atmosphere and should be deliberately integrated into the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evoke place through detail without necessarily naming it
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore: she 'wanted to include... things one might not ordinarily associate with Wisconsin (though I never use the word Wisconsin).'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You can convey a strong sense of place through specifics (local customs, landscape, institutions) without explicit geographic labeling; this can create universality while retaining local texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform autobiographical material; re-contextualize elements
rubrics_metrics.description: On autobiography: 'Oh, there are a few autobiographical things, but every aspect is transformed and re-contextualized.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If drawing on personal life, reshape and fictionalize details so the material serves story and art rather than functioning as thin memoir. Use personal knowledge as a resource, not a literal template.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use emotional truth (e.g., grief) as creative impetus but craft it into story
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore wrote a story prompted by her father's death from Covid: 'Watching him die so alone just broke my heart. And a broken heart of course is often where writing comes from.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Personal grief or strong emotion can generate authentic material; the writer’s task is to shape that material into a rendered, crafted narrative rather than only a record of feeling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely as preparation; write what you want to read
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore: 'I love more than ever... just simply to read, and have started to see it as necessary preparation for writing... Writing should be giving yourself the thing you want to read.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain an active reading practice to inform craft. Let your reading desires guide your writing choices—aim to create the works you yourself most want to encounter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure narrative devices advance the story rather than merely ornament
rubrics_metrics.description: On Rachel Cusk: Moore is 'interested in her use of paraphrase and how it festoons her narrative sometimes rather than advances it.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate stylistic or formal devices (paraphrase, repeated motifs, experimental structures) by whether they contribute forward motion or insight; avoid devices that only decorate without adding narrative value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proofread collected galleys to catch continuity and sequencing issues
rubrics_metrics.description: Moore: she 'didn’t notice continuities or running themes because I didn’t proofread the galleys as I was supposed to' and postponed, missing changes before printing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully proof and review collection galleys—sequencing, continuity, and inter-story relationships can reveal themselves only on close inspection and may require rearrangement or edits before final printing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use alternating settings to structure temporal and thematic contrast
rubrics_metrics.description: About Who Will Run the Frog Hospital?: it 'alternates between a small town in upstate New York in the sixties and post-Cold War Paris.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately shifting settings (times and places) can be used to contrast eras, perspectives, and character development; plan how alternation serves theme and reader orientation.
